meta.description: Oscar Levant, but not in these words — his joke was “a gag,” not “a wisecrack.” Edmund Fuller was the anthologist who wrote it down, not the author.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'An Epigram is Only a Wisecrack That’s Played Carnegie Hall'?
meta.ogDescription: Levant’s quip, first printed in 1941 as “a gag that’s played Carnegie Hall.” The “wisecrack” version is a later editor’s wording.

answer.label: Not Edmund Fuller — Oscar Levant, in different words
answer.authorDates: 1906–1972 · American pianist, composer and professional wit
answer.sourceLine: Levant made the joke; an editor sharpened it. Quote Investigator ↗ finds the two earliest printings in anthologies compiled by Edmund Fuller — Thesaurus of Quotations (1941) and Thesaurus of Epigrams (1943) — and both read “An epigram is a gag that’s played Carnegie Hall,” credited to Levant. “Wisecrack” arrives later: Bennett Cerf’s Laughing Stock (1945) has “a wise-crack that has played Carnegie Hall,” and the exact sentence people quote today is first documented in Evan Esar’s The Dictionary of Humorous Quotations (1949). QI’s verdict: every citation that credits anyone credits Levant, and he is the most likely originator — but the popular wording differs from the earliest instances. Edmund Fuller, who is sometimes named as the author, was the man who wrote it down.
answer.confidenceText: The joke is reliably Levant’s. The wording in circulation is not the wording first recorded.

source.heading: The wording, printing by printing

docMeta.dd: Oscar Levant (1906–1972) — credited in every attributed citation
Edited by Edmund Fuller, Crown Publishers, New York, 1941, p. 331 — wording: “a gag that’s played Carnegie Hall”

source.excerpt: What is an epigram? What sets it apart from the quip, the quiddity, the bon mot… It is Oscar Levant who has definitively scored it for our time with a fine sensitivity to the fact that stuffing is out of place in a humorist’s shirt. By Oscar, “An epigram is a gag that’s played Carnegie Hall.”
trail: Quote Investigator’s article ↗ lays out the sequence with bibliographic detail for each printing: Fuller’s Thesaurus of Quotations (1941, p. 331) and Thesaurus of Epigrams (1943, pp. v and 101), both with “gag”; Cerf’s Laughing Stock (1945, p. 185) with “wise-crack”; and Esar’s Dictionary of Humorous Quotations (1949) with the modern sentence. QI records that it verified the first three on paper.

QI’s conclusion is explicit on both halves: “the most common modern version of the adage uses the word ‘wisecrack’, but the earliest citations located by QI use the word ‘gag’. All the cites credit the phrase to Oscar Levant whenever someone is credited. QI believes he is the most likely originator.” That is why this page credits Levant and still files the wording as disputed.

Levant’s Wikiquote page ↗ carries the line in its own sourced list, as “An epigram is only a wisecrack that’s played at Carnegie Hall,” cited to Coronet magazine, September 1968. Note the extra “at”: even the late wording has not settled into one form, which is what a remembered spoken joke looks like in print.

None of these is Levant publishing his own sentence. He was a radio and television wit whose lines reached print through other people’s collections, so the earliest surviving text is a compiler’s transcription — which is exactly the condition under which a word like “gag” drifts to “wisecrack.”
source.cutTag: Edmund Fuller, introduction to Thesaurus of Epigrams, 1943
source.excerptNote: This is the 1943 passage, and it settles both questions at once: the wording Levant was first recorded using is “a gag,” and Edmund Fuller is plainly the editor quoting him, not the author. Fuller’s own sentence credits “Oscar” by name.

author.name: Oscar Levant
author.heading: About Oscar Levant
author.metaLine: 1906–1972 · American pianist, composer, author and wit
author.bio: Oscar Levant was an American concert pianist, composer, author, actor and comedian, well known for his recorded performances of Gershwin and of numerous classical composers, and a friend of Gershwin himself. He became a national celebrity as a regular panellist on the radio quiz show Information Please and in films such as An American in Paris (1951), where his mordant, self-lacerating wit made him better known for what he said than for what he played. Much of what he is quoted as saying was said aloud and written down by other people — the reason his lines survive in several competing wordings.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Two different things go wrong with this quip: the wrong man gets the credit, and the right man gets the wrong words.

items.why: Fuller edited the Thesaurus of Quotations (1941) and Thesaurus of Epigrams (1943), the two books that carry the earliest known printings. In both, as Quote Investigator ↗ shows, the line is credited to Levant — Fuller’s 1943 introduction names “Oscar” outright. Crediting Fuller mistakes the anthologist for the wit, an easy slip when his is the name on the spine.

items.who: Oscar Levant — but he said “a gag”
items.why: The 1941 and 1943 printings both read “An epigram is a gag that’s played Carnegie Hall.” “Wisecrack” first appears in Bennett Cerf’s 1945 collection and reaches its familiar form in Evan Esar’s 1949 dictionary — see Quote Investigator ↗. The joke survived the edit; the word did not.

A 1955 Georgia newspaper review noted that “perhaps hundreds of persons” had claimed the gag, while confirming it was “originally attributed to Oscar Levant, the vinegar-witted pianist and film star” — quoted by Quote Investigator ↗. Wide repetition is not anonymity.

misattribution.truthLine: Levant made the joke, and he probably made it out loud rather than on paper — which is why the first text of it is an editor’s, and why the word in your version is almost certainly not the word in his, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke only works if Carnegie Hall is unarguably the top of the profession, and it is: one of the most prestigious concert halls in the world for both classical and popular music. It also lands harder from a working musician than it would from a comedian, and Levant was both — a concert pianist and composer, well known for his recorded Gershwin, who ended up far more famous for what he said than for what he played. The line is a musician’s metaphor: the material has not changed, only the room.

There is a nice symmetry in its own history. A quip about a wisecrack being promoted to respectability was itself promoted — from “gag,” the comedian’s word Levant actually used, to “wisecrack,” the tidier one that editors preferred. The sentence demonstrates its own thesis on the way to becoming a quotation.
context.pull: An epigram is a gag that got booked into a better room — and this one did it twice.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI gives the earliest printing as Edmund Fuller’s Thesaurus of Quotations (Crown Publishers, New York, 1941), p. 331, reading "An epigram is a gag that’s played Carnegie Hall," attributed to Oscar Levant.
QI quotes Fuller’s 1943 Thesaurus of Epigrams introduction, which names Levant directly: ‘By Oscar, "An epigram is a gag that’s played Carnegie Hall."’
QI dates the first "wisecrack" wording to Bennett Cerf’s Laughing Stock (1945), p. 185, and the exact popular sentence to Evan Esar’s The Dictionary of Humorous Quotations (1949).
QI concludes all citations credit Levant whenever anyone is credited, and that he is the most likely originator, while the modern "wisecrack" wording differs from the earliest instances.
Wikiquote lists the line in Levant’s sourced section as "An epigram is only a wisecrack that’s played at Carnegie Hall," cited to Coronet magazine, September 1968.

Edmund Fuller’s Thesaurus of Epigrams was published in 1943 (catalogue record). The scan is lending-restricted, so the p. 101 wording was NOT read directly; it is taken from Quote Investigator, which records verifying it on paper.
